lesson.title: Positive Reinforcement: Adding Something to Build a Habit
lesson.summary: Positive reinforcement means adding a desirable stimulus after a behavior in order to make that behavior more likely to happen again.
lesson.body:
In operant conditioning, the words positive and negative do not mean good or bad. They describe whether something is added to the situation, positive, or taken away from it, negative. Positive reinforcement is specifically the case where a desirable stimulus is added after a behavior occurs, and that addition makes the behavior more likely to happen again in the future.

A clean example: a dog sits on command, and its owner immediately gives it a treat. The treat is added, it is the desirable stimulus, and if sitting becomes more frequent as a result, that is positive reinforcement at work. The same pattern shows up constantly outside the laboratory: an employee gets praised for finishing a project early and starts finishing projects early more often, or a student receives a good grade after studying hard and studies hard again on the next assignment.

The single most useful thing to remember about positive reinforcement is the word add. Something is being introduced into the situation, and that addition is what strengthens the behavior. That is what distinguishes it from negative reinforcement, which also strengthens behavior but does so by taking something away instead.
